4.0  Regulatory Setting
The proposed project is located in the City of Palmdale, and noise regulations are addressed through the
efforts of various federal, state and local government agencies. The agencies responsible for regulating
noise are discussed below.

4.1  Federal Regulations
The adverse impact of noise was officially recognized by the federal government in the Noise Control Act
of 1972, which serves three purposes:

    Publicize noise emission standards for interstate commerce
    Assist state and local abatement efforts
    Promote noise education and research

The Federal Office of Noise Abatement and Control (ONAC) originally was tasked with implementing the
Noise Control Act. However, it was eventually eliminated, leaving other federal agencies and committees
to develop noise policies and programs. Some examples of these agencies are as follows: The
Department of Transportation (DOT) assumed a significant role in noise control through its various
agencies. The Federal Aviation Agency (FAA) is responsible for regulating noise from aircraft and airports.
The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) is responsible for regulating noise from the interstate
highway system. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is responsible for the
prohibition of excessive noise exposure to workers.

The federal government advocates that local jurisdiction use their land use regulatory authority to
arrange new development in such a way that noise sensitive uses are either prohibited from being
constructed adjacent to a highway or that the developments are planned and constructed in such a
manner that potential noise impacts are minimized.

Since the federal government has preempted the setting of standards for noise levels that can be emitted
by the transportation source, the City is restricted to regulating the noise generated by the
transportation system through nuisance abatement ordinances and land use planning.

4.2  State Regulations
Established in 1973, the California Department of Health Services Office of Noise Control (ONC) was
instrumental in developing regularity tools to control and abate noise for use by local agencies. One
significant model is the Land Use Compatibility for Community Noise Environments Matrix. The matrix
allows the local jurisdiction to clearly delineate compatibility of sensitive uses with various incremental
levels of noise.

The State of California has established noise insulation standards as outlined in Title 24 of the California
Building Code (CBC) which in some cases requires acoustical analyses to outline exterior noise levels and
to ensure interior noise levels do not exceed the interior threshold. The State mandates that the
legislative body of each county and city adopt a noise element as part of its comprehensive general plan.

5.0  Study Method and Procedure
The following section describes the noise modeling procedures and assumptions used for this
assessment.

5.1  Noise Measurement Procedure and Criteria
Noise measurements are taken to determine the existing noise levels. A noise receiver or receptor is any
location in the noise analysis in which noise might produce an impact. The following criteria are used to
select measurement locations and receptors:
    Locations expected to receive the highest noise impacts, such as the first row of houses
    Locations that are acoustically representative and equivalent of the area of concern
    Human land usage
    Sites clear of major obstruction and contamination
MD conducted the sound level measurements in accordance to the Countys and Caltrans (TeNS) technical
noise specifications. All measurement equipment meets American National Standards Institute (ANSI)
specifications for sound level meters (S1.4-1983 identified in Chapter 19.68.020.AA). The following gives a
brief description of the Caltrans Technical Noise Supplement procedures for sound level measurements:
    Microphones for sound level meters were placed five (5)-feet above the ground for all
  measurements
    Sound level meters were calibrated (Larson Davis CAL 200) before and after each measurement
    Following the calibration of equipment, a windscreen was placed over the microphone
    Frequency weighting was set on A and slow response
    Results of the long-term noise measurements were recorded on field data sheets
    During any short-term noise measurements, any noise contaminations such as barking dogs, local
  traffic, lawn mowers, or aircraft fly-overs were noted
    Temperature and sky conditions were observed and documented

5.2  Noise Measurement Locations
The noise monitoring locations were selected to obtain a baseline of the existing noise environment. Two
short-term 15-minute noise measurements were conducted at the Project site, and long-term data was
extrapolated based on traffic patterns. Appendix A includes photos, the field sheet, and measured noise
data. Exhibit E illustrates the location of the measurements.

5.3  FHWA Roadway Construction Noise Model
The construction noise analysis utilizes the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Roadway Construction
Noise Model (RNCM), together with several key construction parameters. Key inputs include distance to
the sensitive receiver, equipment usage, percent usage factor, and baseline parameters for the project site.

The project was analyzed based on the different construction phases. The construction noise calculation
output worksheet is in Appendix D.

7.0  Future Noise Environment Impacts and Mitigation
This assessment analyzes future noise impacts to and from the project and compares the results to the
Citys Noise Standards. The analysis details the estimated exterior noise levels associated with traffic
from adjacent roadway sources. The project area is outside of any airport 65 dBA CNEL contours and
therefore, there is no aircraft impact.

7.1  Future Exterior Noise
The exterior noise level off-site of the project will be impacted by transportation-related sources and
stationary sources from the site. The following outlines the impacts associated with exterior noise levels.

7.1.1  Future Off-Site Traffic Noise Impact
The project does not require a traffic study, therefore, a full traffic impact analysis is not provided in this
assessment. However, the following provides a brief description of potential traffic noise impact. Traffic
noise along East Avenue S is the main source of noise impacting the project site and the surrounding area.
E Avenue S has an existing ADT of 30,106, per the City of Palmdale Traffic Volume Map. It takes a change of
three (3) dB or more to hear an audible difference, which would occur with a doubling of traffic. The project
is not anticipated to double the traffic volumes along East Avenue S, and the noise impact due to project
traffic will be less than significant.

7.1.2  Noise Impacts to Off-Site Receptors Due to Stationary Sources
Sensitive receptors that may be affected by project operational noise include adjacent residences to the
east, south, and northeast.

On-site operational noise includes transformers and HVAC units. Only the office building will be climate
controlled. HVAC equipment is assumed to be located on the rooftop of the office building. Equipment
will be at least 130 feet away from the nearest residences to the east. The maximum sound power level
from a single unit is 72 dBA. At 130 feet away, the sound pressure level is estimated to be 32 dBA.
Assuming three (3) units are located on the office building and are running simultaneously, the sound
level is 37 dBA Leq. If the units ran simultaneously for 24 hours, the noise level would be 44 dBA CNEL.
This does not take into account the property line wall, which would lower the operational noise at the
residential receptors. According to Policy N-1.3 (Acoustical Analysis for Stationary Noise Sources) of the
Citys General Plan Noise Element, the noise at residential properties must not exceed 65 dBA CNEL. The
worst-case noise due to the HVAC units operating simultaneously will be 44 dBA CNEL, and thus meets
the Citys noise level limit for residential properties. See Appendix D.

Per ANSI and NEPA requirements for transformer noise, transformers must be no louder than 65 dBA at
six (6) feet. Transformers should be placed at least 20 feet from the adjacent residential receptors or
should be shielded to stay below the noise level limit.

Operational noise complies with the Palmdale General Plan Noise Element. The impact is, therefore, less
than significant.

9.0  CEQA Analysis
The California Environmental Quality Act Guidelines establishes thresholds for noise impact analysis as
presented below:

(a) Would the project result in the generation of a substantial temporary or permanent increase in
ambient noise levels in the vicinity of the project in excess of standards established in the local general
plan or noise Code, or applicable standards of other agencies?

Transportation Noise Impacts

The main source of noise due to traffic near the project site is due to traffic from East Avenue S. It takes
a change in noise level of three (3) dB for the human ear to perceive a difference, which takes a doubling
of traffic. The project is not anticipated to double traffic volumes along East Avenue S. Thus, the impact
is not perceptible and the impact is less than significant.

Stationary Noise Sources

Stationary noise impacts would be considered significant if they result in exceedances of 65 dBA CNEL at
residential uses according to Policy N-1.3 (Acoustical Analysis for Stationary Noise Sources) of the
General Plan Noise Element. Implementation of the proposed project may result in stationary noise
related to HVAC Systems. The projected noise level at the nearest residential uses will be 44 dBA CNEL
and will be below the Citys residential noise standard. Thus, the project is less than significant.

Construction is anticipated to occur during the permissible hours as described in the Citys Municipal
Code Section 8.28.030  Construction Noise Prohibited in Residential Zones. Construction noise is
considered a short-term impact and would be considered significant if construction occurs outside the

This letter is in response to the City’s request for trip generation analysis for a proposed self-storage
warehouse on the southwest corner of Avenue S & Cemetery Road in Palmdale, CA. The project will
consist of 725 storage units as shown on the site plan (attached).

Trip Generation

Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation, 11th Edition. The trip generation is based on the ITE
Code 151 (Mini-Warehouse). The results are shown in Table 1.

Vehicle Miles Traveled

In 2013, the state of California enacted legislation (SB 743) which required the Governor’s Office of
Planning and Research (OPR) to recommend new metrics for assessing and mitigating transportation
impacts within the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Regulatory changes to CEQA

Guidelines adopting the use of vehicle miles traveled (VMT) metric were approved on December 28,
2018. Statewide implementation began July 1, 2020.

OPR also released a Technical Advisory on December 28, 2018, which provides guidance related to
the evaluation of VMT as part of a transportation impact analysis under CEQA. The advisory contains
recommendations regarding VMT assessment, significance thresholds and mitigation measures.
Under CEQA, lead agencies have the authority to establish their own VMT significance thresholds and
analysis methodologies or rely on thresholds and methodologies recommended by other agencies,
provided such guidelines are supported by substantial evidence. The VMT analysis for this project
was conducted in accordance with Analyzing Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for CEQA Compliance: SB
743 VMT Implementation Guidelines for the City of Palmdale, dated May 13, 2024.

The City of Palmdale Guidelines identify project types that are presumed to have a less-than-
significant impact on VMT, and therefore, a less-than-significant impact on transportation. The City
of Palmdale Guidelines contain “screening thresholds” for identifying whether a land use project
should be expected to result in a less than significant transportation impact. Projects meeting one or
more of these screening criteria would not be required to undergo a detailed VMT analysis.

One screening threshold pertains to small projects. The City of Palmdale Guidelines states that “…any
other exclusive land use projects or a combination of multiple land uses that in total produce less
than 3,000 metric tons of CO2 equivalent emissions…” are presumed to cause a less-than-significant
impact.

A CalEEMOD model was run using the project trip generation and the report is attached. Based on
the model, the project is anticipated to generate 680 metric tons of CO2 per year. This is below the
threshold of 3,000 metric tons of CO2 per year; therefore, the project is expected to have a less-than-
significant VMT impact.

Subject: Recommended Edits and Additions to Mitigation Measures – CUP 25-0002 / SPR 25-0005 (Mini-Storage
Facility)

Dear Brenda Magaña and Juan Lopez:

Thank you again for coordinating with the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians (FTBMI) on the Mini-Storage
Facility project (CUP 25-0002 / SPR 25-0005), located at the southwest corner of East Avenue S and Cemetery Road in
the City of Palmdale.

Following a detailed review of the IS/MND and consultation materials, the Tribe supports the intent of the proposed
mitigation measures Trib-1 through Trib-3, but respectfully requests the following edits and additions to ensure they
reflect the appropriate level of protection based on our Medium Sensitivity determination.

Requested Additions to the Mitigation Measures (to replace or supplement Trib-1 to Trib-3):

WEAP Training
 Prior to the start of construction, a Qualified representative, procured by the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission
Indians and retained by the Project Applicant, shall conduct a Tribal Cultural Resources Worker Environmental
Awareness Program (WEAP) training for construction personnel regarding the aspects of Tribal Cultural Resources and
the procedures for notifying the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians should Tribal Cultural Resources be
discovered by construction staff.

Training can be done in conjunction with Cultural Resources WEAP training, if such training is requested by the
proposed project’s archaeologist. (This training is about 15 minutes in length)

300-2.3 Treatment and Disposition Plan

A Treatment and Disposition Plan (TDP) shall be established, in consultation with the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of
Mission Indians, prior to the commencement of any and all ground-disturbing activities for the Project, including any
archaeological testing. The TDP will provide details regarding the process for in-field treatment of inadvertent discoveries
and the disposition of inadvertently discovered non-funerary resources. Inadvertent discoveries of human remains
and/or funerary object(s) are subject to California State Health and Safety Code Section 7050.5, and the subsequent
disposition of those discoveries shall be decided by the Most Likely Descendant (MLD), as determined by the Native
American Heritage Commission (NAHC), should those findings be determined as Native American in origin.

300-2.4 Inadvertent Discovery

300-2.4.1 In the Event of an Inadvertent Discovery

If cultural resources are discovered during project activities, all work in the immediate vicinity of the find (within a 60-foot
buffer) shall cease and a qualified archaeologist meeting Secretary of Interior standards retained by the project applicant
shall assess the find. Work on the portions of the Projects outside of the buffered area may continue during this
assessment period. The Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians (FTBMI) shall be contacted about any pre-
contact and/or post-contact finds and be provided information after the archaeologist makes their initial assessment of
the nature of the find, to provide Tribal input with regards to significance and treatment.

300-2.4.2 Disposition and Treatment of Inadvertent Discoveries

The Lead Agency and/or applicant shall, in good faith, consult with the FTBMI on the disposition and treatment of any
Tribal Cultural Resource encountered during all ground disturbing activities.

300-2.5 Human Remains

300-2.5.2 In the Event of Inadvertent Discovery, Human Remains

If human remains or funerary objects are encountered during any activities associated with the Project, work in the
immediate vicinity (within a 100-foot buffer of the find) shall cease and the County Coroner shall be contacted pursuant
to State Health and Safety Code §7050.5 and that code shall be enforced for the duration of the Project.

Inadvertent discoveries of human remains and/or funerary object(s) are subject to California State Health and Safety
Code Section 7050.5, and the subsequent disposition of those discoveries shall be decided by the Most Likely
Descendant (MLD), as determined by the Native American Heritage Commission (NAHC), should those findings be
determined as Native American in origin.

301-2.2 Cultural Resources Monitoring and Mitigation Plan

A Cultural Resources Monitoring and Mitigation Plan (CRMMP) shall be prepared, in consultation with the Fernandeño
Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, prior to the commencement of any and all ground-disturbing activities for the Project,
including any archaeological testing. The CRMMP will provide details regarding the process for in-field treatment of
inadvertent discoveries and the disposition of inadvertently discovered non-funerary resources. Inadvertent discoveries
of human remains and/or funerary object(s) are subject to California State Health and Safety Code Section 7050.5, and
the subsequent disposition of those discoveries shall be decided by the Tribe, as determined by the Native American
Heritage Commission (NAHC), should those findings be determined as Native American in origin.
 301-2.3.1 Full Time Monitoring, Initial Pass, (1) Monitor

The project applicant shall retain a professional Tribal Monitor procured by the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission
Indians to observe all ground-disturbing activities including, but not limited to, clearing, grubbing, grading, excavating,
digging, trenching, plowing, drilling, tunneling, quarrying, leveling, driving posts, auguring, blasting, stripping topsoil or
similar activity during the initial pass (the first disturbance of all soil to the total depth of which it will be disturbed). If
Cultural Resources are not encountered after observing the initial pass of all ground-disturbance, additional Tribal
Monitoring is not required. If Cultural Resources are encountered during the initial pass, the Tribal Monitor(s) shall
observe all remaining ground-disturbing activities, no matter the depth or frequency to which the soil was previously
observed, until all ground-disturbing activities are complete. Tribal Monitoring Services will continue until confirmation is
received from the project applicant, in writing, that all scheduled activities pertaining to Tribal Monitoring are complete,
be it initial pass or all disturbance, dependent upon inadvertent discovery. If the Project’s scheduled activities require the
Tribal Monitor(s) to leave the Project for a period of time and return, confirmation shall be submitted to the Tribe by
Client, in writing, upon completion of each set of scheduled activities and 5 days’ notice (if possible) shall be submitted
to the Tribe by project applicant, in writing, prior to the start of each set of scheduled activities. If cultural resources are
encountered, the Tribal Monitor will have the authority to request that ground-disturbing activities cease within 60 feet of
discovery and a qualified archaeologist meeting Secretary of Interior standards retained by the project applicant as well
as the Tribal Monitor shall assess the find.

Justification for Medium Sensitivity

The Tribe has determined the project site qualifies as Medium Sensitivity due to the following factors:

• Ground disturbance reaching up to 7 feet into native alluvium

• Proximity to documented lithic scatter and midden soils

• Historical lack of AB 52 consultation in surrounding development areas

We respectfully request these recommended measures be incorporated into the final MND. Please let us know if a
redline or tracked version would be helpful for your CEQA file.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the Planning Commission adopt Resolution No. PC-2025-022,
recommending City Council approval of General Plan Amendment (GPA) 25-0002,
Zoning Ordinance Amendment (ZOA) 25-0003, and Zone Change (ZC) 25-0002, and
finding that the project is consistent with Program Environmental Impact Report (PEIR)
22-002 prepared and certified in conjunction with the City’s General Plan (Palmdale
2045).

BACKGROUND

On September 21, 2022, Palmdale 2045 was adopted by the City Council and replaced
the previously adopted General Plan (1993). State law requires that the regulations
governing the use and development of lands within the municipal limits of a city be
consistent with the adopted General Plan for that city. Ordinance No. 1603 was adopted
by the City Council on March 15, 2023, which amended Title 17 of the Palmdale Municipal
Code (PMC) to implement the vision of Palmdale 2045 as well as support new land use.

On August 16, 2023, the City Council adopted Ordinance Nos. 1613 and 1614, which
included minor amendments to the PMC necessary to address inconsistencies, clarify
review procedures, and section references, as well as update the associated Zoning Map.
On December 6, 2023, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1627 was adopted, to
further clarify review procedures within Title 17 related to measuring distance
requirements and uses within the Mixed-Use, Public Facility, and Industrial zones.

On February 7, 2024, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1639, and amended the
Noise Element of the General Plan, the Development Standards for Mixed-Use zones,
the Land Use map, and Zoning map to address inconsistencies and clarify review
procedures.

On June 5, 2024, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1641 to amend and update the
Health and Wellness designation and Medical Flex zone density requirements, Minor
Exception process, Aerospace Industrial zone allowed uses, industrial open space
requirements, and the General Plan Land Use Map and Zoning Map.

On December 22, 2024, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1647 to address and
update review procedures and streamline review processes for City projects.

On July 15, 2025, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1658 to address and update
residential development standards for single-family residences and accessory dwelling
units (ADUs) as required by State law.

On August 19, 2025, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1659 to modify commercial
standards within the Zoning Ordinance.

Since then, City staff has identified further minor amendments necessary to address
inconsistencies and clarify review procedures.

is proposed be changed to Utilities and Rights-of-Way (U-ROW) to be consistent with the

Zoning Ordinance Amendment

When Palmdale 2045 was adopted by the City Council on September 21, 2022, the
Council directed City staff to collaborate with the Mainstreet Coalition to address concerns
raised about the updated commercial development standards in the City. Since then, staff
has been working diligently with the Mainstreet Coalition and have incorporated some
modifications to resolve those concerns within a series of prior Zoning Ordinance
Amendments. ZOA 25-0003 will further amend the special regulations for commercial
uses in PMC Chapter 17.92, specifically Sections 17.92.050 (Drive-through restaurants
and drive-through services) and 17.92.070 (Fueling station/vehicle and equipment
services and repair) to conclude the coordination efforts with the Mainstreet Coalition.

Development standards for new drive-through restaurants will be simplified and
streamlined. Currently, a new drive-through restaurant cannot be located closer than 500
feet from an existing or proposed drive-through restaurant, unless it meets a waiver
requirement, in which case no more than three drive-through restaurants can be located
within a 500-foot buffer, as measured in a straight line from the nearest proposed menu
board to the nearest menu board of the subject property. To simplify this standard, the
buffer will be uniformly set to a 250-foot buffer between the proposed menu board and
any existing or other proposed menu board, and the waiver provision will be eliminated.

Development standards will also be modified for fueling stations to provide flexibility to
the review process. Currently, a new fueling station must be located at a minimum
distance of 500 feet from an existing or proposed fueling station. The proposed revision
will require a minimum distance of 300 feet from an existing or proposed fueling station,
which is measured in a straight line from the nearest proposed fueling pump to the nearest
fueling pump of the subject project, in all directions,.

The proposed amendments address concerns that were raised by the Mainstreet
Coalition group when Palmdale 2045 was adopted and are necessary to clarify review
procedures in a continued effort to streamline processes and provide flexibility. The
proposed amendments provide for public safety, convenience, and general welfare by
allowing for the siting of drive-through restaurants and fueling stations in locations that
are suitable and appropriate by setting buffer requirements and requiring compliance with
the development standards specific to these commercial uses. These changes are
consistent with the goals and applicable policies of the General Plan, as shown in Table
1.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

The project has been determined to be consistent with PEIR 22-002 (State Clearinghouse
# 2021060494), which was prepared and certified by the City Council Resolution No. CC-
2022-096 on September 21, 2022, for approval of the City’s General Plan, Palmdale
2045. As part of the environmental analysis, PEIR 22-002 also considered the adoption
and implementation of the comprehensive zoning update and its associated map. Staff
review has determined that a subsequent or supplemental PEIR as described in California
Environmental Quality Act Guidelines Sections 15162, 15163, or 15164, is not required
because the proposed project modifies the zoning ordinance and the land use and zoning
map to ensure compliance with the recently adopted General Plan and applicable laws,
and would not require major revisions of the PEIR, there are no significant changes in
circumstances and there is no new information of substantial importance that will involve
new significant environmental effects or increase the severity of previously identified
significant effects. As such, staff concluded that the request is consistent with the
previous PEIR in accordance with California Environmental Quality Act Guidelines.

PMC Section 17.92.050.C Development Standards
(1) Site design should locate the drive-through aisle so that pedestrians do not need to
cross the aisle in order to access the main building entrance from the parking lot or street.
If a pedestrian walkway intersects a drive-through aisle, the walkway shall be highlighted
with enhanced paving and lighting and shall be located for maximum visibility of
pedestrians.

(1)(2) Drive-through aisles shall have a minimum 15-foot width on curves and a minimum
12-foot width on straight sections, with a minimum inside turning radius of 15 feet.

(2)(3) Drive-through aisles and structures shall be set back from the ultimate curb face of
an adjacent public right-of-way a minimum of 20 feet, or as otherwise determined by the
Review Authority.

(3)(4) Drive-through aisles shall be screened with a combination of decorative walls and
landscape to a minimum height of 40 inches to prevent headlight glare and direct visibility
of vehicles from adjacent streets and parking lots. Any wall shall comply with sight triangle
requirements of PMC Chapter 17.82 (Setbacks and Location of Buildings) and shall not
be located in a required setback.

(4)(5) Each drive-through entrance and exit shall be at least 100 feet from an intersection
of public rights-of-way, measured at the closest intersecting curbs, and at least 25 feet
from the nearest curb cut on an adjacent property.

(5)(6) Drive-through restaurants and drive-through services within an integrated shopping
center shall have an architectural style consistent with the theme established in the
center. The architecture of any drive-through shall provide compatibility with surrounding
uses in form, materials, colors, scale, and other design elements.

(6)(7) Other than menu boards, signs for drive-through restaurants and services shall
conform to PMC Chapter 17.88.

(7)(8) Drive-through restaurants shall may be required to include a minimum 11-foot-wide
bypass lane, which allows vehicles already served or other vehicles to navigate around a
drive-through lane. A bypass lane shall not include parking spaces. This requirement may
be modified or waived at the discretion of the Review Authority where site constraints
make a bypass lane infeasible.
(8)(9) No new drive-through restaurant use may be approved if located within 500250 feet
from an existing or proposed drive-through restaurant use as measured according to PMC
Section 17.17.020 (Measuring distances).

ANALYSIS

The applicant is requesting that the Planning Commission approve SPR 25-0011 with a
recommendation to City Council for the approval of a form of AGR 25-0002 to construct
eleven, three-story buildings containing 264 dwelling units and three community buildings
totaling 303,143 square feet. The project site consists of one vacant parcel totaling
approximately 9.95 acres and is located at the west side of 15th Street East and
approximately 375 feet north of East Avenue Q. State law requires jurisdictions provide
an inventory of land suitable for residential development as part of its Housing Element
to assist in meeting the City’s Regional Housing Needs Assessment Allocation (RHNA)
and the project site is identified in that list.

The proposed multi-family residential development is located within the Residential
Neighborhood 3 (RN 3) General Plan land use designation and zone. The proposed
development includes site improvements, landscaping, trash enclosures, and community
buildings. The proposed recreational amenities consist of a children's play area, a
swimming pool area, a basketball half-court, a pickleball court, a splash pad, a large dog
play area, a small dog play area, and a vegetable garden for tenants. In addition, there is
a centralized mailroom, maintenance, and laundry room in one amenity building, and a
breakroom for resident services, managers’ offices, conference room, an indoor gym,
learning center, and community room in the second amenity building. Lastly, the project
will provide site improvements such as parking areas, drive aisles, open space, and
landscaping. The development is designed to support a high-density residential
community, consistent with the site’s zone and General Plan land use designation.

Of the proposed 264 dwelling units, 100 percent of the total units will be designated for
households with incomes not exceeding the low-income threshold established by the
California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD). In accordance
with the State Density Bonus Law (Government Code Section 65915), the applicant is
requesting five concessions from the City's development standards to facilitate the
provision of affordable housing.

Density Bonus

Pursuant to the Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC), AGR and SPR approval are required
to allow the proposed development. The project has been reviewed for consistency with
applicable design standards and policies related to density, site planning, circulation,
landscaping, and building form. As a result, the applicant is entitled to and is requesting
multiple incentives and concessions under the Density Bonus Law and PMC Section
17.25.020, as follows:

4  A concession pursuant to PMC Section 17.25.020 (Density Bonus Agreement), to

These requested concessions are intended to facilitate the construction of high-quality
affordable housing while accommodating the site’s physical constraints and design
needs. The project complies with all other applicable zoning regulations and supports the
City’s goals for housing production and affordability.

The Housing Division has determined that granting the concessions listed above will
result in actual and identifiable cost reductions to provide affordable housing. In addition,
the proposed project will contribute to the City’s RHNA allocation.

In addition to the requested concessions, the applicant is requesting three waivers to
facilitate the construction of the proposed project upon recommendation from the
Planning Commission due to financial constraints. The waivers will be reviewed and
approved or denied by the City Council. The applicant has provided their justification for
the waivers requested and are incorporated in the section below:

1  A waiver pursuant to PMC Section 17.25.020 (Density Bonus Agreement), to allow
  for Buildings B, D & F to exceed the 150-feet maximum distance between
  residential buildings and the nearest trash enclosure. Building B and D are 201-
  221 feet from the nearest trash enclosure, exceeding the maximum allowed only
  by 50-100 feet. Furthermore, only 48 units are impacted by this distance exceeding
  the maximum of 150 feet. Due to the current layout of the project, it is physically
  infeasible to rearrange the trash enclosure or residential building locations to
  reduce the distance between the nearest trash enclosures and Buildings B and D
  to 150 feet. Furthermore, adding a trash enclosure to serve only the 48 units in
  buildings B, D & F impacted by the additional 50-100 feet distance to the currently
  placed nearest trash enclosure would pose a cost burden that would exceed the
  current project budget.

2  A waiver pursuant to PMC Section 17.25.020 (Density Bonus Agreement), to allow
  for the leasing office amenity building to exceed the 17-foot height requirement for
  accessory structures. Leasing offices, resident services offices, and the main
  electrical room are necessary for the overall project to operate, and thus cannot
  be removed from the site plan or reduced in size to accommodate the 17-foot
  height requirement for accessory structures. Furthermore, creating an additional
  standalone building to accommodate relocating the second-floor amenities of this
  building would be physically infeasible within the current site plan and would create
  a cost burden that would exceed the current project budget. The estimated cost
  for an additional standalone building is $4,142,857 based on the most recent
  general contractor estimate for structures. This cost overrun would exceed the
  current project budget of $58,000,000 for all 14 current structures.

3  A waiver pursuant to PMC Section 17.25.020 (Density Bonus Agreement), to allow
  for a reduction in the total amount of electric vehicle (EV) charging stations at the
  project site due to Southern California Edison’s (SCE) inability to provide the
  capacity required to power the amount of EV charging stations required by the
  PMC. In order to meet this demand SCE determined that the required upgrades
  will take approximately 45 months to complete. Because this project includes Low
  Income California Tax Credit Allocation Committee (CTCAC) tax credits and
  California Debt Limit Allocation Committee (CDLAC), which require the project to
  begin construction by November 17, 2025 and be completed within less than 45
  months from construction start, it is physically infeasible to provide the full amount

Site Layout

The site layout includes a gated entry for controlled access. In addition to the previously
mentioned amenities, which are centrally located for convenience, the proposal includes
a mailroom, bicycle storage, and laundry facilities. The site also includes nine trash
enclosures spread throughout the property to ensure convenient access and maintain
cleanliness. The layout is designed to balance functionality with walkability.

Access

The project proposal includes street improvements to provide internal circulation as well
as connections to existing roads. Two primary access driveways will be provided along
15th Street East. The City Engineer and Los Angeles County Fire Department have
reviewed the proposed site layout and confirmed that the project is designed to provide
adequate and safe vehicular access.

Architecture

The proposed project features a modern architectural style and incorporates a mix of
durable and visually appealing materials, including cement board panels and metal
panels for siding material, a standing seam metal roof, breeze block veneer, stucco siding
with complimentary colors all of which provide for a clean-lined aesthetic. The design
emphasizes vertical and horizontal articulation to break up massing and add visual
interest throughout the site.

Perimeter fencing utilizes minimalist designs that maintain openness while providing
privacy and security. Amenity buildings vary in design from one-story to two-story
structures with matching exterior finish materials to ensure a unified architectural theme.
The amenity buildings are further complemented with large covered entries to provide
shade and to provide focal points and character of shared outdoor spaces.

Together, the architectural elements of the project reflect a contemporary, high-quality
residential community that provide durable materials and thoughtfully planned amenities
for future residents.

  demonstrate conformance with the City’s intent to encourage attractive and
  context-sensitive residential development

  with the requirements of California Government Code Section 65915 by
  providing the required percentage of affordable housing units in exchange
  for density bonuses and development incentives. The project includes deed-
  restricted affordable units for lower-income households, consistent with
  state-mandated eligibility thresholds. In accordance with Section 65915, the
  applicant has requested concessions and waivers that facilitate the
  development of affordable housing, and the City has verified that all requests
  meet the statutory criteria. As such, the agreement fully aligns with the
  provisions and intent of California's Density Bonus Law.

  D.  Under California Government Code Section 65915, et seq. and Palmdale Municipal
Code Section (PMC) 17.25.020, the City must, upon the request of an applicant, grant a density
bonus and/or certain incentives/concessions and/or waivers/modifications for any development
applicant that seeks and agrees to construct a minimum number of housing units that are affordable
to low or very low income households (the “Density Bonus Law”).

  E.  The subject site has a General Plan Land Use Designation of Residential
Neighborhood 3 and is zoned Residential Neighborhood 3 (RN3) (20-30 dwelling units per acre).
The Density Bonus Law requires that, when an applicant includes at least 20 percent low-income
units, the City must grant a 35 percent density bonus over the base density, which would allow an
additional 10 units per acre in the Residential Development. Therefore, the Density Bonus Law
requires the City to permit the Residential Development’s proposed density of 26.5 dwelling units
per acre. Additionally, in order to provide for affordable housing cost of the low-income units, the
Owner has requested cost-saving concessions in accordance with California Government Code
Section 65915, et seq. and PMC Section 17.25.020, as follows:

ANALYSIS

The applicant is requesting the Planning Commission recommend City Council approval
of a form of AGR 25-0003 and approve SPR 25-0009 to construct thirteen, three-story
buildings containing a total of 272 dwelling units and two recreational amenity buildings
on two vacant parcels totaling approximately 9.8 acres, located at the northwest corner
of East Avenue Q and 25th Street East. State law requires jurisdictions provide an
inventory of land suitable for residential development as part of its Housing Element to
assist in meeting the City’s Regional Housing Needs Assessment Allocation (RHNA) and
the project site was identified in that list.

The proposed recreational amenities consist of an outdoor community gathering area with
a pergola shade structure and barbecue with table seating and benches; a children's play
area; a swimming pool area; and four garden courtyards throughout the site. In addition,
it will provide site improvements such as parking areas, drive aisles, open space, and
landscaping. The development is designed to support a high-density residential
community, consistent with the Mixed Use 3 (MU 3) General Plan land use designation
and zone.

Of the proposed 272 dwelling units, 100 percent of the total units will be designated for
households with incomes not exceeding the low-income threshold established by the
California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD). In accordance
with the State Density Bonus Law (Government Code Section 65915), the applicant at
this time is not requesting any concessions from the City's development standards to
facilitate the provision of affordable housing.

Although the project will be 100 percent affordable and restricted as such under a future
California Tax Credit Allocation Committee (CTCAC) regulatory agreement, the applicant
requests that the project be reviewed and approved as a 10 percent Lower Income
project. The Project consists of 10 percent affordable Lower Income units and qualifies
under Government Code Section 65915(b)(1)(AG) for one concession pursuant to
Government Code Section 65915(d)(2)(AD). At this time, the applicant is not requesting
any concessions.

Density Bonus

Pursuant to the Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC), a Density Bonus Agreement and Site
Plan Review approval are required to allow the proposed development. The project has
been reviewed for consistency with applicable design standards and policies related to
density, site planning, circulation, landscaping, and building form. As a result, the
applicant is not requesting incentives or concessions, but is requesting multiple waivers
under the Density Bonus Law and PMC Section 17.25.020, as follows:
 Staff Report to the Planning Commission

1  A waiver to allow less than the minimum 15-foot front setback and 20-foot rear
  setback requirements.

  The applicant proposed a 10-foot front setback and a nine-foot rear setback. The
  applicants justification is that meeting the development standard would physically
  preclude the project and require the removal of 24 units.

2  A waiver to allow parking garages that are smaller than the required dimensions
  of 10 feet in width by 40 feet in length.

  The project will provide tandem garages that are 10 feet in width by 35 feet in
  length and uncovered tandem spaces that are nine feet in width by 33 feet in
  length. The proposal would provide approximately 42 percent of tandem parking
  spaces. The applicants justification is that meeting the development standard
  would physically preclude the project and require the removal of 24 units.

3  A waiver to allow parking spaces to be located more than 200 feet from the dwelling
  units they serve.

  The applicants justification is that due to the site configuration and building
  typology necessary to achieve 30 du/acre, it is not feasible to meet the max 200-
  foot distance from parking to the unit served.

4  A waiver to allow less than the minimum 30 feet of open-to-the-sky separation
  between structures and/or less than the minimum 30-foot open-to-the-sky building
  break required for buildings over 425 feet in length, subject to approval by the
  Planning Director or designee.

  The project proposes to provide a break between multi-family structures between
  12 feet and 21 feet. The applicant's justification is that meeting the development
  standard would physically preclude the project and require the removal of 48 units

5  An incentive to allow less than the minimum required 125 cubic feet of enclosed
  private storage space per unit.

  The project proposes to provide no private enclosed storage, for which 125 cubic
  feet of storage is required. The total building area needed to comply with this
  requirement is approximately 3,808 square feet, (14 square feet by 272 units =
  3,808 square feet) for the entire project. The applicants justification is that meeting
  the development standard would physically preclude the project and require the
  removal of four to five units.

Site Layout

The site layout includes a gated entry for controlled access. In addition to the previously
mentioned amenities, which are centrally located for convenience, the proposal includes
a mailroom, bicycle storage, and laundry facilities. The site also includes seven trash
enclosures spread throughout the property to ensure convenient access and maintain
cleanliness. The layout is designed to balance functionality with walkability.

Access

The project proposal includes street improvements to provide internal circulation as well
as connections to existing roads. Primary project access will be provided along East
Avenue Q. As identified in the scoping memo accepted by the Traffic Division, a signal
warrant analysis for the intersection of East Avenue Q and 25th Street East will be included
in the required Traffic Impact Study, prepared in accordance with Los Angeles County
Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) Guidelines. The City Engineer and Los Angeles County Fire
Department have reviewed the proposed site layout and confirmed that the project is
designed to provide adequate and safe vehicular access.

Architecture

The proposed project features a cohesive architecture across the project and
incorporates a mix of durable and visually appealing materials, including stone veneer at
the base, two stucco colors, and cement board panels that contribute to a clean-lined
aesthetic. The design emphasizes vertical and horizontal articulation to break up massing
and add visual interest throughout the site.

Many residential units include tandem garage spaces located on the ground floor,
supporting both functionality and efficient land use. Perimeter fencing utilizes minimalist
designs that maintain openness while providing privacy and security. The pool house and
clubhouse are designed as one-story structures with matching stone veneer to ensure a
unified architectural theme. These are further complemented by a pergola shade structure
that reflects the overall project design, enhancing both the usability and character of
shared outdoor spaces.

Together, the architectural elements of the project reflect a contemporary, high-quality
residential community that provide durable materials and thoughtfully planned amenities
for future residents.

  A  The proposed density bonus agreement is consistent with the maps and

  B  The City’s General Plan and any applicable Specific Plan. (SPR)

  C  The development standards set forth in this Title. (SPR)

  The proposed project as demonstrated in Exhibits C and D, is consistent with
  the Mixed Use 3 (MU 3) General Plan land use designation and zone, which
  allow for high-density residential development on the project site. The project
  meets applicable land use, density, and development standards, and no
  General Plan amendments or zone changes are required. The project site is
  located within the City’s Regional Housing Needs Assessment Allocation
  (RHNA). Additionally, the project supports the City’s goals for increasing
  affordable housing and promoting compact, infill development in areas served
  by existing infrastructure and transit, further aligning with General Plan
  objectives. As demonstrated in Exhibit D, the proposed project meets the
  density, lot size, lot width, and lot depth requirements of the MU 3 zone, and
  is therefore suitable for the type and density of the proposed development.

  The proposed project complies with the applicable development standards
  set forth in Title 17 of the PMC, except where deviations are allowed pursuant
  to Government Code Section 65915 (Density Bonus Law). The project meets
  all baseline zoning requirements for multifamily residential development,
  including height, setbacks, parking, and open space standards, or has
  received appropriate waivers as permitted for qualifying affordable housing
  projects. These waivers are necessary to physically accommodate the project
  and do not result in any adverse impacts to health, safety, or the physical
  environment. In addition, the proposed project is consistent with the City’s
  applicable design guidelines for multifamily residential development. The site
  layout emphasizes connectivity, security, and convenience through features
